newsitem.title: MEXICO: INTERVIEW -Mexico left claims big electoral boost.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW -Mexico left claims big electoral boost.

text.p: Mexico's main left-wing opposition claims rising support and expects to capture a fifth of the votes in congressional elections next July, for its best performance yet, if current trends continue, a senior party official told Reuters.

The Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) has had a checkered electoral history since its formation in 1989. But a string of recent local election advances have breathed new life into a party some analysts were writing off only a year ago.

The PRD expects to poll a "minimum" of 21 percent nationally in July, sharply up from nine percent in Mexico's last midterm congressional races in 1991, Leonel Godoy, the PRD's chief election strategist, said in a telephone interview.

Godoy said his party was benefiting from stronger leadership, voter discontent with the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), and a "halo" effect from its candidate for mayor of Mexico City, Cuauhtemoc Cardenas.

"The effect of the successful campaign of Cuauhtemoc Cardenas in Mexico City has pulled in sectors of the population who are now supporting the PRD in places where we weren't significant before," Godoy said.
"For example in the states of Sonora, Nuevo Leon, Queretaro and San Luis Potosi, published surveys show that our support has risen by up to 100 percent compared to what it was," he added.
Most polls give Cardenas a big lead over his opponents in the mayor's election, which will be held July 6, the same day as the congressional races.
All of those north and north-central states hold governors' races on July 6 as well as electing federal congressmen.
"We estimate our maximum possible vote at 35 percent," he said. "We think all three parties in congress will be around the 30 percent level but we want to be the biggest one of these."
Under Mexican election rules, a party needs only 42 percent of the national vote in order to win a majority in the lower house, the Chamber of Deputies.

President Ernesto Zedillo's PRI has so far said its support stands around the 42-45 percent level but the opposition claim they have a good chance of destroying the PRI's lower house majority for the first time ever.

Asked about the governors' races, Godoy said the PRD had the best chance of winning what would be its first governorship in the small southeastern state of Campeche. It was also strong in Colima but had no realistic chance in the other four states electing a local leader.
Asked where most of the PRD's extra support was coming from, Godoy said: "We think most of those now voting for the PRD are the nationalistic sector of Mexico who traditionally voted for the PRI".

Some middle-class voters who chose the conservative National Action Party (PAN) in 1994 presidential elections were also defecting to the PRD, fed up with what Godoy termed the "errors" of the PAN such as its alleged religious intolerance and conservative morality.

The PRD changed leaders last August and Godoy said its new national chief, Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador, had lifted voter support by stressing party unity and oiling the PRD's electoral machinery and local organisation.
Godoy also praised Zedillo for being more tolerant of the PRD, in contrast to his predecessor Carlos Salinas de Gortari.
"Salinas treated us as an enemy to be exterminated...while the Zedillo government has allowed us more freedom and room for manoeuvre," Godoy said. "They treat us as political adversaries."
